summary: Specifies a padding convention for the AES Key Wrap algorithm of RFC 3394, allowing keys of any practical length to be wrapped, not just multiples of 64 bits. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5649 extends AES Key Wrap so it can protect key data whose length is not a multiple of 64 bits. It adds zero padding and records the original length so the receiver can verify and remove the padding.

subtitle: A padding extension that lets AES Key Wrap protect key data whose length is not a multiple of 64 bits.

tldr.problem: The original AES Key Wrap algorithm requires at least two 64-bit input blocks, so some key lengths do not fit its input format.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5649 pads key data on the right with zero octets and stores its original length in an Alternative Initial Value with a distinct constant.
tldr.outcome: The extension supports key data from one octet through 2^32 octets with AES key-encryption keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits. Unwrapping checks the constant, length, and padding.

today: RFC 5649 is Informational and was published in August 2009. It extends the AES Key Wrap algorithm described in RFC 3394; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Wrapping Keys of Different Lengths
sections.content:
Key wrapping uses one key to encrypt and integrity-protect another key. The AES Key Wrap algorithm in RFC 3394 requires input key data to contain two or more 64-bit blocks.

RFC 5649 removes the requirement that the key data length be a multiple of 64 bits. The key-encryption key must be a 128-, 192-, or 256-bit AES key. Input key data can be from one octet through 2^32 octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The original AES Key Wrap accepts only certain input lengths. This extension allows key data of any practical length, including data shorter than one 64-bit block.

sections.title: Length and Padding Information
sections.content:
The Alternative Initial Value (AIV) is 64 bits. Its high-order 32 bits contain the constant A65959A6; its low-order 32 bits hold the original key-data length in octets, most significant octet first.

If the input length is not a multiple of 8 octets, the sender appends the fewest zero octets needed to reach a multiple of 8. During unwrapping, the receiver checks the constant, verifies that the length fits the recovered blocks, and confirms that all padding octets are zero. Failure of any check returns an error.
sections.plainLanguage: The AIV records the original length and contains a constant that distinguishes this method from unpadded AES Key Wrap. The receiver checks both before removing zero padding.

sections.title: Wrapping and Unwrapping
sections.content:
The wrapping process pads the plaintext to a whole number of 64-bit blocks and uses the AIV as the initial value. If the padded plaintext is exactly one 64-bit block, the AIV and block are encrypted together as one AES block, producing two 64-bit ciphertext blocks.

For longer input, the process applies the AES Key Wrap steps from RFC 3394 to the padded blocks using the AIV. Unwrapping reverses the process, validates the AIV and padding, then returns the number of octets recorded in the length field.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender pads and wraps the key data together with its length information. The receiver unwraps it, checks the recorded length and padding, and returns the original key data.

sections.title: Key Protection and Algorithm Use
sections.content:
The key-encryption key must be protected because someone who obtains it may disclose every key wrapped with it. The RFC says the key-encryption key should be at least as strong as the material it protects; effective protection is limited by the weaker algorithm.

The padded and unpadded algorithms use different initial-value constants, so one format cannot be successfully unwrapped as the other, even when no padding was needed. The RFC says the method provides almost the same integrity protection as the original and should be used only for cryptographic keying material.
sections.plainLanguage: Protect the key-encryption key because it can reveal the wrapped keys. Use key wrap for cryptographic keying material, not for other data.
